They must instead be defined, as Hegel did and Marx, Lenin, and Stalin followed him in doing, “in the image of the human being.”

In other words, we must say that human beings possess a special quality that belongs to them alone and that can, if one wishes, be called non-natural—though certainly not supernatural. It is philosophy’s task to determine what this quality is.
In this respect Christian pseudophilosophy did make some progress, particularly in recognizing the essential importance of human work.

But because it began from the theological idea of god inherited from pagan philosophy—an idea that still had a “thing-like” character—the purely philosophical, or anthropological, contribution of Christianity and Judaism remained extremely slight.
37) In this respect, the Phenomenology resembles Descartes’s Discourse on the Method.
38) For example, even if we know all the qualities common to iron, we still will not know what distinguishes one particular piece of iron from another, or why.
The common qualities of natural things are such that knowing them gives us no clue to their particular differences.
Aristotle even turned this into a logical principle: knowledge of the particular includes knowledge of the general, but knowledge of the general does not include knowledge of the particular.
If I know this piece of iron, I also know iron in general. But the reverse does not follow.
39) This is what is true in “materialism.”

But genuine materialism must not be confused with vulgar “materialism,” which forgets that not everything that exists is material, simply because everything concrete and everything that actually exists is in some sense material.
Alongside real existence there is also “ideal” existence, as we will see.
Between the realm of concrete, real, material being and complete non-being lies the extraordinarily rich and varied realm of abstract, ideal, “non-material”—though not “spiritual”—being.

Here we find, for example, the mathematical world of points, figures, numbers, formulas, and so on; the world of fictional characters such as Chichikov and his kind; the world of general abstract concepts such as iron in general, humanity in general, the State in general; and much else besides.
All of these things unquestionably exist. Yet it is equally unquestionable that they do not exist materially, or really.
Human beings live directly in both realms. Through the body, we are immersed in the real world; through discourse, or logos, we are immersed in the ideal world.
But the ideal world does not exist without human beings, and human beings do not exist without material bodies.
It is only in this sense that we can say that everything that exists is either itself material or depends on something material.
That is materialism properly understood—the materialism we find in Hegel and Marx, and later in Lenin and Stalin as their successors.
We should therefore not be misled by the sometimes incorrect use of the term found in all four writers.
40) As I have already said, we must understand the word “matter” in a broad sense.

From the standpoint of physics, a space that is “empty” but contains an electromagnetic field has no “matter” in the narrow sense, but it does contain “energy,” which is likewise measured in CGS units.
In our terminology, then, this simply means that there is “matter” there.
The word “mass,” however, must be understood to include not only “effective mass” but also “inertial mass.”
It is true that from the standpoint of relativity theory there is hardly any essential difference between these two masses—that is, between energy and matter.
Our terminology can therefore coincide with that of contemporary physics.

Science holds that only what can be measured in units of time, space, and mass can act directly.
Magic holds that a word—or indeed any kind of being, including things that cannot be measured—can act directly.
When an engineer “builds” a bridge, the first thing he does is draw plans. In that sense we can say that the bridge exists because of the plans.
But it exists because of them only indirectly. Without the material efforts of the workers, there would be no bridge.
A “magician,” by contrast, believes that one can draw plans which will somehow build themselves, without the mediation of other people.
That is the entire difference between magic and technology.

These qualities are, of course, eternal and unchanging.
But every concrete table, even though it itself changes, also possesses “eternal” and unchanging qualities that distinguish it from every other concrete table.
All of its changes together form a pattern belonging uniquely to that table and belonging to it “forever”—that is, for as long as it exists.

To think otherwise is to think “magically.”

For now I will say only this: by giving things names, human beings move them from material being into ideal being.
This concrete tree, for example, became “the tree in general”—an abstract, general concept—when the “first” human being pointed to it and said “tree.”
And by understanding such a word, a human being can move in the opposite direction, from ideal existence to real existence.
Thus a carpenter who understands the word “table”—that is, the abstract concept—can make a real, material table.

The abstract character of “what is common” passes from the ideal world into the human being, but it does not pass into the material world.

That is why, as we have already noted, knowledge of humanity in general—or of the general concept “human being”—includes knowledge of individual human beings, whereas knowledge of the general concept of a thing does not include knowledge of the differences between the material things that fall under that concept.
The human being is therefore not a thing, but an “entity” of another kind.

So if we want to know everything about a particular electron, we must also know where it is and therefore where it stands in relation to the rest of the world.
Exactly the same applies to my desk.

It is not, just as non-being is not—and there can be no knowledge of non-being beyond the knowledge that it is not.
The ideal world, meanwhile, has no time.
But in the real world, knowledge of the present already includes knowledge of the future, insofar as the laws of nature are expressed as analytic functions.

50) Or, more precisely, I would know that I am not a “sage”—insofar as I cannot give a meaningful answer to every question about myself—precisely because I am this particular individual who does not fully know who he is.
51) This can be maintained at least until the eighteenth century.

It was only in the nineteenth century, after the rapid development of the individual sciences, that some philosophers began to regard philosophy itself as one particular science with its own special field of knowledge, rather than something that included the whole of knowledge in general.
52) I know, of course, that there really are things about which I know nothing while nevertheless knowing that they exist.
Consequently, these things in their concreteness include my knowledge of them, even if that knowledge amounts only to knowing that they exist without knowing what they are.
This is undeniable, and it has nothing to do with “idealism.”
Idealism claims that my knowledge “creates” things and that without me they would cease to exist.
In reality, all we can say is that the things I actually know do not, as a matter of fact, exist without my knowledge of them—although they obviously could exist without it.

My desk includes both the weight of my hand resting on it and my knowledge of the desk. If we “abstract away” either that weight or that knowledge, we turn the concrete table before us into an “abstract” desk.

53) It has long been recognized that the so-called “secondary” qualities—color and appearance, for example, as opposed to weight and shape—do not exist apart from human beings, or more generally apart from living beings equipped with sense organs.
Physics, however, deals with the “primary” qualities, such as space, time, and mass, and so might seem to deal with “things in themselves,” independently of humanity.
Contemporary quantum physics has shown that this is not so.

Heisenberg’s “uncertainty principle,” for example, would make no sense if physics did not take into account the fact that, for physics, only things we can observe exist—that is, things we can observe with our eyes, by means of light.
The electron therefore stands in relation to a human “observer” in exactly the same way as a mountain or the color of a desert does.
Even in geometry, the “observing subject” is represented by a coordinate system.
But this book is hardly the place to discuss all of that.
I will therefore say only that in physics itself, the attempt to “abstract away” the subject leads to obvious physical errors.
Even so, contemporary physics does not become philosophy merely because it includes the subject in its investigations.
The subject it includes is not a concrete human being, but an abstraction—an eye “in general,” or even an idealized eye.
So although physics includes the observer, it still “abstracts away” the fact that the concrete subject not only sees but also always “feels,” “acts,” and so on.
54) All of this will become clearer only later.
For now I will simply note that the conception of the human being as an essentially historical entity, rather than as a thing possessing eternal qualities, was first stated clearly by Hegel.
Marx adopted the same conception, notably when he spoke of the “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom.”

But this conception, like Hegelianism as a whole, had been quietly prepared by Judeo-Christian theological thought, whereas the conception of the human being as a thing goes back to pagan Greek philosophy and science.

A medieval Jewish thinker, for example, could be convinced that the difference between a Jew, a member of the “chosen people,” and a “goy,” a non-Jew, was so great that the two should not even be brought together under the same concept of “human being.”
That opposition between Jew and goy is obviously absurd.

But it is true that the difference between people belonging to different historical worlds can be so great that knowing the qualities they have in common does not amount to knowing what constitutes their specifically human, or historical, essence.
55) We now know that the system of definitions and axioms attributed to “Euclid” does not exhaust all geometrically possible systems of definitions and axioms.
There are also non-Euclidean geometrical “things”—triangles, for example, whose angles add up to more or less than two right angles.

But this does nothing to undermine the truth of Euclidean geometry, because from the outset that geometry seeks to study only those geometrical “things” that satisfy the definitions and axioms laid down by “Euclid.”

It is true that, as the work of Hilbert and others has shown, drawing up the complete list of axioms with no unnecessary elements—and above all proving that the system contains no contradiction—is an extraordinarily difficult task requiring in practice an immense amount of work.
But in principle there is no insurmountable difficulty here.
56) As I have already said, geometrical “axioms” are not in any sense self-evident truths.
When applied to real space, they are only hypotheses, since we are still far from knowing the geometrical structure of our actual space, which is very probably not Euclidean.
Within pure geometry, meanwhile, “axioms” are simply “postulates,” or definitions of the objects to be studied. It therefore makes no sense to ask whether they are true or false.
Lobachevskian geometry, for example, is neither more nor less “true” than “Euclidean” geometry.

The choice of mathematical “axioms” is completely arbitrary. They need only avoid contradicting one another and form a closed system corresponding to a definite group of “things” that exist “mathematically,” or ideally.
